summary: Explains the seed objects that IANA needs to create and digitally sign to support hierarchical delegation of objects in the Internet Routing Registry for RPS Security, and lists the operations required. Its status is historic, and it was replaced by RFC 6254.

plainLanguage.summary: It describes the first signed entries at the top of a registry so everyone below can be trusted. It is now historic.

subtitle: Setting up the root of the routing registry hierarchy with digital signatures.

tldr.problem: The Routing Policy System (RPS) requires hierarchical delegation of objects in the Internet Routing Registry (IRR), but the root of that hierarchy needs to be established and digitally signed by IANA.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2754 specifies the seed objects IANA must create and sign (a maintainer, key certificate, and the root allocation blocks for AS numbers and IP addresses), and defines the operations IANA must perform as it makes new allocations.
tldr.outcome: This document was published as informational to guide IANA in setting up RPS security, but the approach was superseded by RFC 6254 with updated procedures.

today: RFC 2754 is Historic and was superseded by RFC 6254. It describes procedures that were used in early RPS deployments but are no longer current.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Routing Policy System provides a way for networks to describe their routing policies and be delegated pieces of the IP address and AS number space in a way that other networks can verify as authentic. This requires a hierarchy of trust: just as a company signs contracts with its authority over them, IANA must digitally sign the root objects in the registry to establish that it owns the entire space.

This document specifies the objects that IANA needs to create at the root of the RPS hierarchy and describes the operations required each time IANA makes new allocations to regional registries or other parties.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of IANA as a notary public who signs that 'yes, this organization really owns this range of network numbers.' This explains what IANA needs to sign and keep signed.

sections.title: Initial Seed Objects and Assignments
sections.content:
IANA must distribute a public key with RPS software implementations. An initial set of seed objects—a maintainer object (mnt-iana), a key certificate object, and the root AS and IP number blocks—must be signed with this key and distributed as a single signed transaction.

Each time IANA makes an allocation (such as assigning AS numbers to a regional Internet registry or IP ranges), it must create corresponding inetnum and as-block objects and sign them with its key. These objects must include the status (ALLOCATED) and the name of the delegated organization.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA starts by publishing its own signed statement of 'I own all AS numbers and all IP addresses.' Then every time IANA gives some to someone else, IANA signs that delegation too.

sections.title: Creating Routing Repositories
sections.content:
When a new routing registry is created (such as a regional registry), IANA must create and sign three objects on its behalf: a maintainer object, a key certificate object, and a repository object. The maintainer object specifies who can update objects within that repository. The key certificate holds the registry's public key, and the repository object describes how to query and submit updates.

This very first transaction for a new repository is placed in the new repository itself, not in IANA's repository, giving the new registry its initial authority to operate.
sections.plainLanguage: When a new registry starts (like a regional one), IANA signs documents giving it permission to hand out its own ranges and make its own rules. This gives the new registry 'authority' over its corner of the system.

sections.title: Security and Future Work
sections.content:
The security of the RPS system depends on IANA's key being kept secure and the signatures being generated only by authorized IANA staff. This document specifies the seed objects and operations needed to maintain the root of the authorization hierarchy.

The document notes that the IANA assignments must follow proper procedures and that the separation of duties between IANA and the registries is critical to the integrity of the system.
sections.plainLanguage: The whole system only works if IANA's signing key is secret and trustworthy. IANA must follow careful procedures when signing new delegations.
